scene.narration: Say you want to find seventy two in this list. If you do not know the list is in order, all you can do is check every box, starting from the first.

steps.say: Is it two? No.
Is it five? No.
Eight? No.
And so on, until the eleventh box finally holds seventy two.
If the number sits at the very end, or is not there at all, you check all sixteen. For four billion rows, that is four billion checks.
We can do much better, if the list is sorted. That one rule is the whole trick.

scene.narration: Instead of starting at the front, put one pointer at each end.

steps.say: L marks the start, at index zero. R marks the end, at index fifteen.
Halfway between them is index seven.
It holds forty five. Now ask one question. Is seventy two equal to it, smaller, or bigger?
Why not just add L and R and halve it? On a huge list, that sum can get too big for the number type in Java or C, and wrap around. Taking half the gap from L never gets that big.

scene.narration: Here is where the order pays off.

steps.say: The target is bigger than forty five.
Every box left of it is even smaller. So none of those first eight can be the one. We cross them all out in one go, and L jumps to index eight.
Find the new middle. It is index eleven.
It holds seventy nine. The target is smaller.
So index eleven and everything right of it are out. R moves to index ten.
Sixteen boxes went down to half, and now just three are left, after only two looks.

Three before the third. Each look also throws out the middle box, and the two sides are not always equal, so this search went sixteen, eight, three, one.
And one box for the last look.
In general, every look halves what is left. Halve n about log two of n times, and one box is left. So doubling the list adds just one more look.

scene.narration: Say you want the cheapest way to get from S to E. Each arrow is a one way road, and its number is what that road costs.

steps.say: S is where we start, and E is where we want to end up.
One way is S to A, then A to E. That costs four plus six, which is ten.
Another is S to B, B to C, then C to E. That costs two plus five plus one, which is eight.
Checking every route works on five places. On a real road map with millions of crossings, there are far too many routes to try.
Dijkstra's method keeps a table instead. For each place it notes the cheapest cost found so far, the place you came from, and whether that cost is settled.

scene.narration: Say you keep ten million phone numbers, and you need to find one of them, again and again, thousands of times a second.

steps.say: In a list with no order, you may have to check every one of the ten million.
Sort the list and you can halve it on each check, so twenty four checks are enough.
That is fast. But when a busy system does this thousands of times a second, even twenty four checks add up.
What we want is one jump, straight to the spot where the number lives. No scanning, no halving. That is what a hash table gives you.

scene.narration: The trick is to work out the spot from the key itself. The rule that does this is called a hash function.

steps.say: Our key is the word cat.
Every letter is stored as a number. C is 99, a is 97, and t is 116.
Add them up, and you get 312.
The table has only eight slots, so we keep the remainder after dividing by eight. 312 divided by eight leaves 0.
So cat goes in slot zero.
To find cat later, we do not search. We do the same sum, get zero again, and read slot zero.

scene.narration: With chaining, the danger is a crowded table. Here seven keys sit in eight slots, and each list hangs down below its slot.

steps.say: The load factor is the number of keys divided by the number of slots. Seven over eight is zero point eight seven five.
The keys do not spread out evenly, so the lists grow. Slot zero holds 3 keys, and finding pig means walking past cat and act first.
So the table grows. We make a new one with twice the slots, sixteen.
Then every key is hashed again, this time with the remainder after dividing by sixteen, and moves to its new slot. Most lists shrink to one key.
Cat and act still share slot eight, because their sums are equal whatever the size. Real hash functions mix in the order of the letters, so this happens far less.

scene.narration: Many tables grow once the load factor passes about two thirds to three quarters. Then the lists stay short, and every operation is one jump plus a check or two.

steps.say: On average, looking up, adding and removing all take the same short time, however big the table gets.
The worst case is every key in one slot, which a good hash function makes very unlikely.
Growing the table is slow when it happens, but it happens so rarely that it adds only a little to each insert on average. That is how dictionaries, database indexes and caches answer in an instant.

Is forty two sorted? Yes. A single item is always in order.
Merge sort uses that. It breaks the list down until every piece is one item, then stitches the pieces back together in order.

scene.narration: Quicksort is a divide and conquer sort. It picks one value, called the pivot, and moves everything smaller to its left and everything bigger to its right. Then it does the same thing to each side.

steps.say: In this version, the pivot is always the last item. Here that is five.
After one split, the four smaller numbers sit on the left, and the three bigger ones on the right.
Five is now exactly where it belongs in the sorted list. It never moves again.
The two sides are still jumbled, so quicksort splits each of them the same way.

scene.narration: Here is how one split works. The pointer j walks the list from left to right. The pointer i marks the end of the small pile, shown in green, and it starts just before the list. Bigger numbers turn amber.

steps.say: j looks at seven. Seven is not smaller than five, so it stays put.
j moves on to two. Two is smaller than the pivot, so it belongs in the small pile, which starts at the first cell.
So i steps forward, and the two swaps into the small pile.
Nine is bigger, so j just moves past it.
Four is smaller. The next spot in the small pile holds seven.
i steps forward, and four swaps places with the seven.
One is smaller too, and the next spot holds nine.
So one swaps with the nine.
Eight is bigger. Skip it.
Three is smaller, and the next spot holds seven.
Three swaps with the seven.
Now every number before the pivot has been checked. The spot right after the small pile holds nine.
So the pivot and the nine swap.
Five lands at index four. Smaller on its left, bigger on its right. That is its final resting place.

Eight and seven are both smaller, so nine stays at the end.
Then the two cells left of it, with pivot seven.
Seven swaps in front of eight, and eight is left on its own. The whole list is sorted.

scene.narration: How fast is it? Each round of splits touches every item about once. So the speed depends on how many rounds there are.

steps.say: When the pivot lands near the middle, each row halves the pieces. Eight items take three rounds, which is log two of eight. That gives n log n, both on average and at best.

But give it a list that is already sorted. The last item is always the biggest, so each split peels off just one item. That makes about n rounds, and the time grows with n squared. This is the worst case.

scene.narration: Picture a busy city the way a ride app sees it. Every driver and every rider is a dot, and the city is cut into districts.

steps.say: The districts come from old maps, like postcodes. Their borders are jagged, and no two are the same size.
Each dot is a pair of numbers, a latitude and a longitude, and it moves every few seconds.
This car sits right on the border between two of them. Cross the street, and it lands in the other one, with a different price.
To learn if a point is inside Old Town, draw a line out from it and count how often it crosses Old Town's outline. It crosses once, an odd number, so the car is inside.
The database does this for every car. Each check walks every corner of every border it tests.
With thousands of cars asking every few seconds, the query falls behind and times out.

scene.narration: Picture a busy city the way a ride app sees it. Every driver and every rider is a dot, and the city is cut into districts.

steps.say: The districts come from old maps, like postcodes. Their borders are jagged, and no two are the same size.
Each dot is a pair of numbers, a latitude and a longitude, and it moves every few seconds.
This car sits right on the border between two of them. Cross the street, and it lands in the other one, with a different price.
To learn if a point is inside Old Town, draw a line out from it and count how often it crosses Old Town's outline. It crosses once, an odd number, so the car is inside.
The database does this for every car. Each check walks every corner of every border it tests.
With thousands of cars asking every few seconds, the query falls behind and times out.

scene.narration: Only three regular shapes cover a flat map with no gaps: triangles, squares and hexagons. Look at how far away each cell's neighbours are.

steps.say: A triangle touches twelve others, at three different distances. That makes "nearby" messy.
A square has four neighbours along its sides, all at the same distance, call it d.
But the four corner neighbours are about one point four times as far. Forty one percent farther, yet they still count as next door.
A hexagon has six neighbours, and every one is exactly the same distance away. No corner problem, so spreading things out to nearby cells stays even.

scene.narration: The earth is a ball, and hexagons alone can't cover a ball. So H3 starts with a twenty sided shape inside it.

steps.say: Put a shape made of twenty triangles inside the ball, touching it at its corners.
Cut it open and lay it flat. Each triangle becomes a flat map of its own patch of the earth, and hexagons tile each one.
There's a catch at the twelve corners, where five triangles meet. A rule about closed shapes says some cells must have five sides, and here it's exactly twelve.
So every level has twelve pentagons. H3 turns the shape so all twelve land in the ocean, where nobody calls a car.

scene.narration: Here is one big hexagon. H3 fills it with smaller hexagons, then fills each of those again.

steps.say: Start with one big cell.
Seven smaller cells sit inside it: one in the middle and six around it.
Seven hexagons only make a big hexagon shape when they're turned, so each level sits turned about nineteen degrees from the one above.
Do it again, and each of the seven holds seven more. Forty nine.
The fit isn't perfect. The small cells poke out past the big one's edge a little, and that's fine for counting cars.
H3 repeats this sixteen times, from level zero to level fifteen.

scene.narration: Each level is about seven times smaller in area than the one above. Uber picks the level that fits the job.

steps.say: The biggest level has a hundred and twenty two cells for the whole planet. The smallest is under one square metre.
Matching happens at level nine, where a cell is about two hundred metres across an edge. That's about a city block.
Surge pricing looks at levels seven and eight, where many blocks are counted together.
To go from a level nine cell to the level seven cell that holds it, you don't touch the map. You just change a few bits in its name.

scene.narration: Every H3 cell has a name that fits in one 64 bit number. This one names a cell in downtown San Francisco, at level eight.

steps.say: The first bits are housekeeping. The mode is one, which says this number names a cell.
Four bits hold the level. Here it's eight.
Seven bits say which of the hundred and twenty two biggest cells it sits in. Here it's number twenty.
Then come fifteen digits of three bits, each from zero to six. Each digit says which of the seven smaller cells to step into, one step at a time. This cell takes eight steps, so it uses eight digits.
Levels this cell doesn't reach hold a seven, all three bits on, which means not used.
To get the parent one level up, set the level to seven and mark the eighth digit not used. A few bit changes, and no map lookup.

scene.narration: A rider asks for a car. Instead of measuring the distance to every car in the city, the app looks at cells around the rider.

steps.say: The rider is in this cell. Its name is one number.
First, look up the six cells that touch it. Each is one lookup in a table of cars by cell. No cars there.
Widen by one ring. That's twelve more cells, nineteen in all, and three cars.
Only those three cars go to the routing engine, which works out real driving times on real roads.
Cars farther out are never even looked at.

scene.narration: Here is what the switch bought Uber. They released H3 as open source in 2018.

steps.say: Finding a car's area went from checking border edges to reading a number.
Pricing areas went from jagged districts to even hexagons.
A place went from two sixty four bit numbers to one, a whole number you can group by and compare.
And rolling small cells up into bigger ones went from merging shapes to changing a few bits.

scene.narration: Alice wants PrintMyPhotos to print some pictures from her Google account. Years ago, the only way was to give the app her Google password.

steps.say: Alice types her real password into PrintMyPhotos.
The app logs in to her Google account, pretending to be her.
Problem one: it opens everything. The app could read her Gmail and Drive, or delete her photos.
Problem two: her secret now sits in their database. If they get hacked, it leaks.
Problem three: to cut the app off, she has to change her password, which logs out everything else too.
OAuth fixes this. It is about what an app may touch, here just the photos. It is not about proving who someone is.

steps.say: Both keys start the car, so the valet can do the job.
But you keep the master key. The valet only borrows the weak one, for the evening.
And it cannot open the trunk or the glove box. An OAuth token is that valet key.

scene.narration: Before anything else, the app makes a secret of its own. This trick is called PKCE, said pixie. It proves later that the same app is asking.

steps.say: The app picks forty three random characters, the code verifier. It keeps this secret on the phone.
It runs that through SHA-256, a hash that cannot be run backwards, and gets thirty two bytes.

That text is the code challenge. The challenge goes out, and only the app knows what made it.

scene.narration: Here is the whole round trip, from the first hop to the app holding a token.

steps.say: The app sends Alice’s browser to the sign-in service, challenge and all.
Alice signs in on Google’s own page and sees what the app wants: to view her photos. She taps allow.
Alice comes back to the app with a one-time code. Not the token itself, because web addresses leak, into history and logs.
The app swaps the code for a token in a direct request, and sends the secret along.
The sign-in service hashes the secret. If it matches the challenge from before, this is the same app that asked.
Then it hands over the tokens. Alice’s password never went near the app.

steps.say: The app hands in the one-time code.
And the secret itself, the verifier. Only the app that made the challenge knows it.
Back comes an access token, the valet key.
It lasts thirty six hundred seconds, which is one hour.
And a refresh token, for getting a new key later without bothering Alice.

steps.say: The token starts its sixty minutes.
Half an hour in, requests still work.
At sixty minutes the API says no: four oh one, unauthorized.
The app sends its refresh token to the sign-in service and gets a fresh access token.
Alice never sees a thing. And if a token leaks, it stops working within the hour.

scene.narration: Every web page is a tree of elements the browser keeps in memory, called the DOM. Changing it by hand is where apps get slow.

steps.say: Say our code finds the list and replaces its inner HTML.
The browser now has to work out every size and position again, then repaint. That is called a reflow.
And each element is not a small thing. Inside the browser, one list item carries hundreds of properties, styles and listeners.
Change fifty list items in a loop, and read a size after each one, and the browser redoes the layout fifty times. Everything stutters.
React’s idea: you describe what the page should look like for your data, and React makes the fewest changes to get there.

scene.narration: React 16 rewrote this as Fiber. Each component gets a small object, a fiber, with three links: its first child, its next sibling, and its parent, called return.

steps.say: A loop holds one pointer, work in progress. It starts at App.
It does App’s work, then follows the child link down to Header.
Header has no child, so it follows the sibling link across to Main.
Now say a click comes in. The loop just stops. The pointer remembers where it was, and the browser handles the click.
Then it picks up right where it left off, down to Card.
Card has no child and no sibling, so it climbs back up the return link to Main.
Main has no sibling either, so up again to App. Back at the top, the walk is done.

scene.narration: Every update now happens in two phases.

steps.say: The render phase calls your components and works out what changed. The commit phase applies it.
Render can pause, give up, or start again. Commit never stops once it begins.
Render never touches the page. Commit changes it all in one go.
And straight after, commit updates refs and runs layout effects.

scene.narration: React keeps two trees: the one on screen, and the one it is building.

steps.say: The root’s current pointer marks tree A, the one the user sees, where the count is one.
In the background, render builds tree B, with the count at two. The user sees none of it.
When it is done, commit applies the changes and swaps one pointer. The new tree is now current.
So the user never sees a half finished page. Tree A is kept, to build the next update in.

scene.narration: And someone then watches it on a phone in a train, or on a 4K TV at home.

steps.say: Uploads arrive in every format and size you can imagine.
They pile up by the petabyte, every day, and old videos still have to be kept.
And every play has to start fast and never stall, on a weak phone signal or on fast fiber.
So we draw a line down the middle. On one side, the control plane: small web requests, like titles, search and likes.
On the other side, the data plane: moving huge video files. These are two different problems, and they get different machines.

They pile up by the petabyte, every day, and old videos still have to be kept.
And every play has to start fast and never stall, on a weak phone signal or on fast fiber.
So we draw a line down the middle. On one side, the control plane: small web requests, like titles, search and likes.
On the other side, the data plane: moving huge video files. These are two different problems, and they get different machines.

scene.narration: A creator uploads a four gigabyte file from their laptop. Sending it as one huge request would be fragile.

steps.say: So the app cuts the file into 500 pieces of eight megabytes and sends them one after another, through the gateway.
The ingestion service writes each piece to blob storage as it arrives.
Then the Wi-Fi drops halfway through piece two.
When it comes back, the app asks how much arrived. Sixteen megabytes. It carries on from there, instead of starting the whole file again.
When the last piece lands, the service drops a message on a Kafka queue: a new video is ready. The upload is done, and processing can start whenever there is room.

scene.narration: A 4K file is far too big for a phone on a weak signal. So workers make several smaller versions of it.

steps.say: A free worker takes the next job off the queue.
It splits the work into branches, one per size: 1080p, 720p, 480p and 360p. Each one is a smaller file.
Every version is then cut into short chunks, four seconds each, so a player can switch between them at any chunk.
Last, it writes a manifest: a small text file that lists every version and where its chunks are.

scene.narration: Now someone watches on a phone. The player, not the server, picks which version to fetch for every chunk.

steps.say: On good Wi-Fi, the player fetches the first chunk in 1080p.
It times every download. Still fast, so chunk two is 1080p too.
Then the train enters a tunnel, and the next download crawls.
At this speed a 1080p chunk would take 12.5 seconds to load, longer than it plays. So the player looks at the manifest and asks for 480p, which loads in 3.5.
The picture gets softer for a while, but the video never stops to buffer.

scene.narration: Chunks are plain files that never change, which makes them perfect for a content delivery network, a CDN.

steps.say: Every video lives at the origin, a big data center, here in the middle of the United States.
Edge servers sit close to viewers, in cities like New York, Frankfurt, Singapore and Tokyo.
A small slice of videos gets most of the views. Their chunks stay on the edge servers, so a viewer in Tokyo gets them from Tokyo, not across an ocean.
The long tail of rarely watched videos is not kept everywhere. When a viewer in Frankfurt asks for one, the edge fetches it from the origin, and keeps a copy for a while.

scene.narration: The control plane has its own stores. The video itself is never in them, only facts about it.

steps.say: Titles, channels and upload times go in a database that spreads across many machines and still keeps them consistent.
Search works the other way round. An index lists, for every word, the videos that contain it, from their titles, descriptions and transcripts.
Search for cat piano, and it looks up both words and keeps the video that is in both lists: number eighty seven.

Search works the other way round. An index lists, for every word, the videos that contain it, from their titles, descriptions and transcripts.
Search for cat piano, and it looks up both words and keeps the video that is in both lists: number eighty seven.

scene.narration: Counting views sounds easy. Now imagine a video going viral, with a hundred thousand views every second.

steps.say: The simple way: every view runs one update that adds one.
But each update locks the row while it writes. A hundred thousand of them a second just queue up behind each other, and the database falls over.
The fix: count in memory first. Each view bumps a counter in Redis, which is very fast.
Once a second, a bot check throws out the fake views, and one single update adds what is left to the row.

scene.narration: Let’s put it all together.

steps.say: The creator uploads in pieces through the gateway, into raw storage.
An event on the queue wakes the transcoders, which write chunks and manifests.
The CDN keeps popular chunks near viewers, and each player picks the version its connection can carry.
And beside all that, the small stuff: views counted in memory before they are written, titles in a database, and words in a search index. Two planes, each built for its own job.

scene.narration: Here is the thing most bread recipes do not tell you. Every ingredient is really just a percentage of the flour.

steps.say: The flour is always one hundred percent. Say we use 500 grams.
Water is sixty six percent of that, so 330 grams.
Salt is two percent, 10 grams.
And yeast is one point two percent, just 6 grams.
Add the percentages up and you get more than a hundred, 169.2. That is fine. It just means the dough weighs 846 grams.

scene.narration: So what changes if you go drier or wetter? Here is the same flour at sixty and at eighty percent.

steps.say: Only 100 grams of water separate these two.
At sixty percent the dough is firm and easy to handle. At eighty it is slack and sticky.
The drier one bakes up tight and chewy. The wetter one is moister inside, and stays fresh longer.
But a wet dough takes more skill to shape, and longer in the oven.
Which is why bagels and pretzels are stiff doughs, and big rustic loaves are wet ones. Sixty six sits comfortably in between.

scene.narration: And here is why bakers love percentages. Scaling a recipe stops being a headache.

steps.say: Want two loaves? Double the flour, and every other number doubles with it.
Want exactly 1200 grams of dough for a big pan? Divide it by one point six nine two, the total percentage. That gives 709 grams of flour, and the percentages do the rest.

scene.narration: Now the method. The times come from a tested recipe for this same kind of dough.

steps.say: Mix everything and knead for about 6 minutes, until it is smooth.
Cover it and let it rise until it has doubled. That takes one to two hours, depending on how warm your kitchen is.
Shape it into a loaf.
Let it rise again, about 45 minutes.
Bake it hot, four hundred and fifty Fahrenheit, for twenty to twenty five minutes.
And let it cool before you cut it. It is still cooking inside.

scene.narration: Here are the parts involved. The new piece is a rate limiter, which caps how many requests one visitor can send.

steps.say: The limiter keeps its counts in Redis, a shared in-memory store, so every server sees the same numbers.
The limiter does not handle a Redis outage. If Redis is down, the limiter fails, and so does every order.
The orders service, the code that saves orders, now asks the pricing module for prices before it writes to the database.
The event queue is also new. Other services read the queue to learn about new orders.

scene.narration: Here is the order of calls for one order request.

steps.say: The request reaches the rate limiter first. The limiter asks Redis to add one to this visitor's count.
Then the orders service gets the prices and saves the order.
After the save, the API puts an order created message on the queue. The API waits until the queue accepts the message, not until another service acts on it. Then the API answers the client.

scene.narration: Start with something simpler. A few friends pay for each other’s dinners, and they keep one shared list of who paid whom.

steps.say: Alice pays Bob twenty dollars, so she writes it down.
More lines go on the list as the month goes by.
At the end of the month they settle up. Whoever is down puts cash in a pot, and whoever is up takes cash out.
But anyone can add a line. What stops Bob from writing that Alice pays him a hundred dollars?

scene.narration: The fix is a digital signature. Each person makes a pair of keys: a secret key they never share, and a public key everyone can see.

steps.say: Alice runs her line and her secret key through a signing function. Out comes a signature, a string of five hundred and twelve bits.
Anyone can check that signature against the line and Alice’s public key. The answer is true.
If Bob changes the line, the old signature no longer fits, and the check says false. Without Alice’s secret key, he cannot make a new one.

scene.narration: Here are real signatures made with one secret key. Watch what happens when the line changes.

steps.say: This is Alice’s signature for paying Bob a hundred dollars.
Change one character, a hundred to a hundred and one, and the signature looks completely different.
Put the old signature on a changed line, and the check fails.
But Bob can still copy the whole signed line, word for word. The copy checks out, so Alice would pay him twice.
So every line gets a number of its own, and the signature covers that number too.
Now a copy carries a number that is already on the list, and everyone ignores it.

scene.narration: Signatures stop fake lines, but not debt. Charlie could run up a huge bill and vanish. So add a rule: everyone starts with a hundred, and a line counts only if the list shows the payer has the money.

steps.say: Charlie pays Alice sixty. He can cover it, so the line counts, and he has forty left.
Charlie pays Bob forty. That leaves him with nothing.
Alice pays David twenty. She has plenty.
Then Charlie tries to pay David thirty. Read the list from the top, and he has nothing left, so everyone rejects that line.
Notice that nobody holds any dollars now. The money is just the list, so call it ledger dollars. Owning some means the history says you have them.

steps.say: So drop the website. Instead, everyone keeps their own copy of the list.

Now the copies disagree about the order. With no one in charge, how does everyone agree on one history?

scene.narration: The answer needs one more tool, a hash function called SHA-256. It takes any text, short or long, and gives back two hundred and fifty six bits, written here as sixty four hex digits.

steps.say: This is the hash of Hello, with a capital H.
Change just that one letter to lower case, and the whole result changes. Nothing about it is close to the first.
And there is no way back. To find text with a given hash, all you can do is guess, and the guesses would outlast the universe.

scene.narration: Now a puzzle. Take a batch of lines, add a number called a nonce, and hash the lot. The goal is a hash that starts with thirty zero bits.

steps.say: With a nonce of zero, the hash starts with only 1 zero bit.
So try one, then two, then three. Each guess gives a hash that looks random.
Our computer kept going for a few minutes, and this number finally worked. Each bit halves the odds, so thirty zeros takes about two to the thirty guesses, around a billion.
Finding it is slow, but checking it is fast. Anyone can hash the lines with this nonce once and see the zeros.

scene.narration: Lines are grouped into blocks. A block counts only if it solves the puzzle, and each block starts with the hash of the block before it. That links them into a chain.

steps.say: Block one’s hash starts with the zeros its nonce bought.
Block two writes that hash at its top. So does every block after, about the one before it.
Now say someone changes an old line in block one, ten to a hundred. Its hash changes completely, and no longer starts with zeros.
Block two still points at the old hash, so the link is broken, and everyone can see it.
To hide the change, the cheat must solve the puzzle again for block one, then for every block after it.

scene.narration: People called miners collect the lines everyone broadcasts and race to solve the puzzle for the next block.

steps.say: Maya solves it first. The first line of her block pays her ten ledger dollars out of thin air. That reward is the only way new money appears.
But Omar solved a different block four at nearly the same moment. Now there are two chains of the same length.
The next miner happens to build on Maya’s block. That chain is longer now, and the rule is simple: everyone follows the longest chain. Omar’s block is dropped, and its lines go back into the pool.

scene.narration: Here is the attack. Alice pays Bob in one block, while secretly building another chain where that payment never happened. If her chain gets longer, everyone switches to it, and her money comes back.

steps.say: But her one machine races everyone else’s together. Say she has a tenth of all the computing power.
If Bob waits for one block on top of his payment, her chance of ever catching up is about one in five.
Each extra block makes it much smaller. After six blocks it is about two in ten thousand. So Bob waits a few blocks before he trusts the payment.

scene.narration: That is Bitcoin. The network adjusts the puzzle every two thousand and sixteen blocks, about two weeks, so a new block comes about every ten minutes.

steps.say: In two thousand and nine, each block paid its miner fifty bitcoin.
Every two hundred and ten thousand blocks, about four years, the reward halves. Twenty five, then twelve and a half, then six and a quarter.
Since twenty twenty four it is three point one two five. Add up every halving and the total stops just short of twenty one million bitcoin.
Blocks also have a size limit, so people add a small fee to their line, and miners pick the lines that pay them best. As the reward shrinks, fees pay more of the miners’ bills.

steps.say: First the text is cut into tokens. A rare word gets split into smaller pieces.
Each token is swapped for a long list of numbers that stands for its meaning. The model looks it up in a big table.
Then the tokens talk to each other. The word model means something different after machine learning than after fashion.
Next, each token's numbers go through the same set of questions, all at once. These two stops take turns, again and again.
At the end, the last token's numbers are turned into a score for every token the model knows.
And one last step turns those scores into chances that add up to one hundred percent.

scene.narration: Each token's list of numbers is a point in a huge space. GPT-3 uses 12,288 numbers per token. Here is a flat sketch of the idea.

steps.say: Words with close meanings end up close together. Near tower you find skyscraper, spire and lighthouse.
Directions mean something too. The step from man to woman is about the same as the step from king to queen.
Take sushi, add the step from Japan to Germany, and you land near bratwurst.
There's even a direction for plural. Multiply two lists number by number and add it all up, and the total tells you how much they point the same way.

scene.narration: At first, a token's numbers only mean the word itself. As they pass through the layers, they soak up the text around them. Take the word king in a play by Shakespeare.

steps.say: Before the first layer, king just means king.
A few layers in, it has picked up that this king rules Scotland.
Deeper still, it holds the story: he got the crown by murder.
By the last of GPT-3's ninety six layers, it even knows the style is old poetry. This is a rough picture, not what the numbers literally say.

scene.narration: Every few minutes the timeout job looks at each pending order and decides what to do with it.

steps.say: The job loads each order that is still pending.
If the payment has arrived since, the job leaves the order alone.
If not, the job checks whether the order is older than a day.
An unpaid order older than a day is cancelled, and its stock goes back on the shelf.
The cancelled order is finished.

scene.narration: Five settings change with the new lifecycle.

steps.say: New orders now start as pending instead of paid.
A pending order gets twenty four hours to be paid.
A job looks for expired orders every five minutes.
A declined card is retried three times instead of never.
The refund window goes away with the refunded state.

scene.narration: Checkout no longer waits for the charge to settle, so it gets faster across the board.

steps.say: Fast, typical and slow checkouts all get quicker.
The typical checkout drops from three hundred twenty to one hundred eighty milliseconds.
The slowest one percent falls from two point four seconds to under a second. The card charge now finishes in a background job.

scene.narration: When a card is declined, the pay job retries with doubling waits.

steps.say: The first charge is declined.
Two seconds later, the job tries again.
Then the job waits four seconds before the second retry.
After eight more seconds comes the third and last retry.
Then the job gives up. The order stays pending until the customer pays, or the timeout cancels the order.

scene.narration: Here is the same order, side by side, under the old rules and the new ones.

steps.say: A new order used to start as paid. Now a new order starts as pending, until the money arrives.
When a card is declined, the old flow gave up at once. The new flow retries three times.
An order nobody pays for is now cancelled after a day, instead of staying open forever.
The stored order drops the refund date and gains an expiry time.
Shipping does not change. A paid order ships just as before.

scene.narration: The API passes every request through a stack of checks, from top to bottom, in the order shown here.

steps.say: A new order request first passes the server's shared checks, which add security headers and read the body.
The session check finds the signed-in user, so the request goes on.
Next comes the new rate limiter, which counts how many requests this user sent in the last minute.
Past a hundred requests, the limiter answers too many requests by itself and sends that straight back.
So the route, the order logic and the database never see the extra requests at all.

When the customer then swaps tea for cake in the cart, the order changes too.
The fix gives the order its own copy of the list, so later cart edits leave the order alone.

scene.narration: Here are those rules as five gates: two XORs, two ANDs and an OR. This circuit is called a full adder.

steps.say: Take the right-hand column: a one on A, a one on B, and no carry in.
The first XOR asks, is exactly one of them on? No, so it outputs zero. The first AND asks, are both on? Yes.
The second XOR mixes in the carry. Zero and zero, so the sum is zero.
And the OR passes the first AND's one out as the carry. One plus one: write zero, carry one.

scene.narration: Now copy that full adder four times, one per column, and wire each carry out into the next column's carry in.

steps.say: Each box is the same five gates we just traced.
The ones column gets one and one. It writes zero, and passes a carry one to its left.
The twos column could not start until that carry arrived. Zero, one and the carry make two again: zero, carry one.
The fours column: one, zero and the carry. Again zero, carry one.
The eights column has only the carry, so it writes one, and nothing carries out.
Each carry had to wait for the one before it, rippling from right to left. That's why this is called a ripple carry adder.

But seven percent growth with three percent inflation is about 3.9 percent of real growth. Seventy two divided by that is about 19 years, and the exact answer is 18.2. That is how long it takes to double what your money can actually buy.

scene.narration: The customer sits outside. The support team owns the ticket, and engineering helps when the problem is a bug.

steps.say: The story starts with one customer who has a problem.
The customer writes to the help desk, and the message lands with one support agent.
That agent owns the ticket until it is resolved, whoever else helps.
The agent checks the help guides first, because most problems already have a known fix.
When the guides have no answer, the agent and the on-call engineer work on the problem together.

The guides do not cover the problem. So the agent hands the ticket to the engineer, with every detail already gathered.
The engineer corrects the tax rate and the billing system reissues the invoice.
The fix goes back to the agent, who tells the customer and sends the new invoice.

scene.narration: The new helper wraps any function so that it only runs once the calls stop coming.

steps.say: The helper takes the function to run and how long to wait. By default it waits two hundred fifty milliseconds.
It keeps a single timer, shared by every call.
Each new call cancels the wait started by the call before it. So while you keep typing, nothing runs.
When a quarter second passes with no new call, the timer fires and runs the function once, with the last text you typed.
A cancel function drops a search that is still waiting, so a closed search box sends nothing.

scene.narration: A website can remember who you are in two ways. It can put everything in a signed cookie that your browser carries, or keep it on the server and give you only a ticket number.

steps.say: With a signed cookie, the browser holds the whole session. With a server session, it holds only a random id.
Here is what each cookie looks like. One carries the user and their role, the other just a number.
The big difference is signing out. A stolen signed cookie keeps working until it expires. A server session can be deleted at once.
The cost is one extra read per request. In return there is no size limit.
Both are equally safe on the wire, as long as the cookie is marked secure.

scene.narration: A small blog keeps its writing in five tables. Here is what each one holds, and how they point at each other.

steps.say: Each post has one author, and one author can write many posts.
A post with no publish date is still a draft, so nobody else sees it.
A comment belongs to one post and one user, so it points at both.
Posts and tags meet in a small table in the middle. Each row says this post has this tag, so a post can have many tags and a tag many posts.

A new test checks the defaults, and that a missing setting is named.

scene.narration: When your browser needs a product photo, it asks a stack of places in order, nearest first. Here is a first visit, when none of them has the photo yet.

steps.say: The browser looks in its memory first. Nothing there on a first visit.
Then in its disk cache. Not there either.
So the request goes to the nearest edge server of the CDN. On a busy shop, this is where nearly every photo is found.
This time the edge does not have it, so it asks our own servers, which read the original from storage and shrink it.
On the way back up, the edge keeps a copy for a week.
And the browser keeps one too, so the next time this photo shows at once.

scene.narration: Most of the border between the United States and Canada is one line of latitude.

steps.say: In 1818 the two countries drew it along the forty ninth parallel, from the Lake of the Woods to the Rocky Mountains.
West of the mountains the land stayed open to both until 1846, when the Oregon Treaty carried the line on to the coast.
Right at the end, the straight line cuts the tip off a Canadian peninsula.
That tip, Point Roberts, is American soil, reached by land only through forty kilometres of the country around it.

scene.narration: In Python, giving a list a second name does not make a second list.

steps.say: After b equals a, both names point at the same list.
So changing b's second item changes a's too.
Copying the list gives b a list of its own, and the two stop sharing.

scene.narration: Every call to factorial gets a frame of its own, stacked on the one that called it.

steps.say: Factorial of three needs factorial of two, so a new frame goes on top.
That needs factorial of one, which is the base case.
It returns one, and its frame is gone.
Then the last frame finishes with six.

scene.narration: Four copies of one right triangle, with short sides a and b and long side c, sit inside a square whose side is a plus b.

steps.say: The space they leave in the middle is a tilted square on the long side, so its area is c squared.
Now slide three of the triangles. None of them turns, and the big square stays the same.
The space left is now two squares, one on side a and one on side b.
The same four triangles left both spaces, so c squared equals a squared plus b squared.

scene.narration: The grey line jumps between one and minus one. We will build it out of smooth sine waves.

steps.say: One sine wave already rises and falls in step with the square wave.
In the middle it reaches 1.27, too high.
Add the next two odd waves and the shoulders flatten. The middle drops to 1.10.
Five waves, and the sides get steeper.
With fifteen it hugs the square wave, 1.021 in the middle.
Except right at the jump, where it overshoots to 1.18. More waves move that bump closer to the jump, but never shrink it.

scene.narration: Put ten thousand dollars somewhere that grows seven percent a year, and leave it alone.

steps.say: Year by year it bends upward, to $76,123 after thirty years.
It doubles in about ten years, to $19,672. The rule of seventy two says the same.
But prices rise three percent a year. In today's money the thirty year total is worth $31,361.
The shaded gap is what inflation takes.

scene.narration: Follow one session through a morning with a lunch break.

steps.say: Signing in starts a thirty minute idle limit.
Each page they open pushes that limit back by another thirty minutes.
Then they go to lunch. Thirty minutes after the last page, the session ends.
Back from lunch, they sign in again, and the browser's old cookie is cleared.

scene.narration: Here is the new list function, from what it takes to what it gives back.

steps.say: It takes a cursor called after, and a page size of fifty by default. Small thing, after here actually means older than, since the newest come first.
The query keeps events strictly older than the cursor. I think this is a bug. A second event with the very same time as the cursor is never shown.
When the page is full, the time of its last event becomes the cursor for the next page.
It now gives back an object with the events and the cursor, where it used to give back a plain list. Old clients that expect a list will break.

scene.narration: When you press sign in with Google, four parties pass messages back and forth. Your password only ever goes to Google.

steps.say: You press the button. The shop sends you on to Google, with a random value it will check later.
You type your password on Google's own page, never on ours. Google sends you back with a short-lived code.
The shop checks that the random value is the one it gave you, so nobody can slip you their own code.
The shop trades the code for your email address, straight with Google.
It finds your account, or makes one, and signs you in.

scene.narration: A pull request is a proposed change to the code. Here are the states it can be in, from the first draft to merged or closed.

steps.say: It starts as a draft, which nobody is asked to look at. When the author is ready, it goes into review.
A reviewer can ask for changes. The author pushes fixes, and it goes back into review. This loop is where most of the time goes.
A plain comment does not change the state at all.
Once approved, any new commit sends it back into review, so the reviewer sees the final code.
An approved pull request merges only when all its checks pass. Merged and closed are the two ways it ends.

steps.say: We tell git which commit is bad and which was good. It picks the commit halfway between.
Then git runs the checkout test at each stop by itself. Here the test fails, so the bug is in the older half.
At the next stop the test passes, so the bug is in the newer half of what is left.
Seven test runs later, git names the first bad commit, the free shipping discount.
That commit touched one file, the shipping code, so that is where to look.

scene.narration: The sales report job starts every thirty minutes. On Tuesday night one run took far longer than usual, and here is what happened.

steps.say: Run one starts at two in the morning, and on a normal night it ends twelve minutes later.
That night the database was slow, so run one was still going when run two started.
For twenty two minutes, both runs added the same sales to the report, so some rows were counted twice.
Run one finally ended after fifty two minutes.
The fix makes each run take a lock first. Run three waits for run two to finish, then writes a correct report.

scene.narration: Let’s go down the spec sheet one row at a time, and give each row to whichever board wins it.

steps.say: The processor. The Pi five has a newer core, the A seventy six, and runs it at 2.4 gigahertz instead of 1.8. First point goes to the five.
Graphics and memory both go to the five as well: a new graphics chip that runs Vulkan, newer memory, and up to sixteen gigabytes of it.
The two camera and display ports are now twice as wide, and each one takes either a camera or a screen.
USB and networking are the same on both. That one is a tie.
Power is where the four wins. The five wants a five amp supply, so your old 3 amp charger may not cut it.
The five is rated to run hotter, up to 70 degrees, and it will be made for two years longer. Final score, 6 to 1.

Then the endpoint makes a reset token. I think the logging line is risky. The log gets the whole token, and anyone who holds that token can change the user's password.
Finally it emails the reset link to the user and answers that the request was accepted.

scene.narration: Start with your phone, sitting on the ground.

steps.say: Your phone has no idea where it is. It has to be told.
Twenty thousand kilometres up, a ring of satellites circles the planet. The drawing is to scale.
Each one moves at almost four kilometres a second, and goes all the way round in just under twelve hours.
Every satellite carries an atomic clock, and keeps sending out the time. The signal takes about a fifteenth of a second to reach you.

scene.narration: Your phone compares the time in each signal with when it arrived. The gap, times the speed of light, is how far away that satellite is.

steps.say: One distance puts you somewhere on a circle around the first satellite.
A second and a third circle cross at just one point.
That point is you. Out in three dimensions, a fourth satellite also corrects the cheap clock in your phone.
Now make one satellite’s clock a millionth of a second late. Light goes three hundred metres in that time, so that circle lands three hundred metres off, and the crossing point moves.

At about nine and a half thousand kilometres from the centre, the two effects cancel exactly.
GPS orbits much higher, so gravity wins, by thirty eight point six.
Further out the curve flattens, as both effects fade.

scene.narration: So the engineers do something strange. They make the satellite clocks wrong on purpose.

steps.say: Tuned like the ground clock, the satellite clock creeps ahead, a little more every day.
So before launch, it is tuned a hair slow: four parts in ten billion.
Up in orbit, relativity speeds it up by exactly that much, and seen from the ground it ticks in step.
Orbits are not perfect circles, so your phone adds one last small correction, up to about twenty three billionths of a second. Relativity is not just a theory here. It is in your pocket.

scene.narration: The vaccine does not contain the virus. It holds only a message: the instructions for the spike, written in mRNA.

steps.say: The message is fragile, so it travels wrapped in a tiny bubble of fat.
The bubble merges with the outer skin of a cell near the shot, and slips inside.
There it lets go of the message.
A ribosome, the cell’s protein maker, grabs it and reads it three letters at a time.
For every three letters it adds one building block to a chain, until the whole spike is built.
The cell folds the spikes and carries them out to its surface, where they stick out like flags.
Then the cell breaks the message into pieces and gets rid of it. Its job is done.
And notice where the message never went: into the nucleus, where your DNA is kept.

steps.say: The virus lands in your nose and starts looking for cells to enter.
Memory cells recognise its spikes straight away.
They multiply and pour out antibodies much faster than the first time.

The virus is stopped before it can spread far. The message that taught your body is long gone. Only the memory stays.
